content.thinking:
I’ve just finished writing the core files for the Earth digital twin: the HTML skeleton, CSS styling, and the main JavaScript that sets up the Three.js scene, loads textures, computes solar position, etc. The next logical step is to make sure everything I’ve downloaded actually arrived correctly before I try to run the app. If any of the texture files are corrupted or incomplete, the WebGL renderer will fail to load them and the page will show errors or blank textures. Likewise, the Three.js library files need to be verified that they are indeed the expected JavaScript files and not some HTML error page or truncated download.

I already have the texture files in `D:\physics\earth\textures` and the library files in `D:\physics\earth\lib`. The simplest sanity check for the JPEGs is to look at their magic numbers – the first three bytes should be `FF D8 FF` for a valid JPEG. I can script this in PowerShell: list all `.jpg` files in the textures folder, read the first three bytes of each, format them as hex, and output a line showing the magic bytes, filename, and file size. This will quickly tell me if any of the downloads are corrupted.

In addition, I want to peek at the beginning of the `three.module.js` file to confirm it looks like JavaScript code rather than an HTML error page. I can read the first few lines (say, three lines) and take the first 80 characters, which should include the module header and maybe a comment. That will give me confidence the library is correct.

Both checks can be done in a single PowerShell command: first compute the JPEG diagnostics, then concatenate a separate command that extracts the first part of the library file. PowerShell allows me to separate statements with a semicolon, so I can run the JPEG loop and then the `Get-Content` pipeline. I’ll store the JPEG files list in a variable `$files`, iterate with `foreach`, read the bytes via `[System.IO.File]::ReadAllBytes`, slice the first three bytes, format each as a two‑digit hex string, join them, and output a formatted string showing magic, name, and size. After that loop, I’ll pipe `Get-Content` on the `three.module.js` file, limit to the first three lines, select the first line, and take its first 80 characters.

This combined command will give me a concise verification of both the texture assets and the core library before I spin up a local server. It’s the most efficient next step, so I’ll issue a PowerShell tool call with exactly this command.

arguments.command: $files = Get-ChildItem D:\physics\earth\textures\*.jpg; foreach ($f in $files) { $b = [System.IO.File]::ReadAllBytes($f.FullName)[0..2]; $magic = ($b | ForEach-Object { $_.ToString('X2') }) -join ''; "{0}  {1}  {2:N0} bytes" -f $magic, $f.Name, $f.Length }; (Get-Content D:\physics\earth\lib\three.module.js -TotalCount 3 | Select-Object -First 1).Substring(0,80)
arguments.description: Verify JPEG magic bytes and lib download
